docs.title: pinnrl
docs.text:
Physics-informed neural networks for forward and inverse PDE problems, evaluated against numerical references.

A physics-informed neural network (PINN) represents the solution u(x, t) of a PDE as a neural network. It is trained to make the PDE residual, the boundary conditions and the initial condition vanish at sampled collocation points, optionally together with measured data. No mesh is needed, and the PDE's parameters can be learned alongside the solution.

pinnrl packages that workflow:

  • your own equations, written as text: CustomPDE("u_t + u*u_x - nu*u_xx", ...) for PDEs, ODEs, steady problems and systems (Custom equations);
  • ten shipped PDE configurations: heat (1-D and 2-D), wave, Burgers, convection, KdV, Allen–Cahn, Cahn–Hilliard, Black–Scholes and a damped pendulum. Each exact solution is checked against its PDE, initial condition and boundary conditions by the test suite.
  • seven network architectures;
  • adaptive collocation sampling;
  • adaptive loss weighting;
  • inverse problems (parameter identification);
  • data-driven training on The Well datasets;
  • a Dash dashboard for launching and inspecting runs.
pip install pinnrl
pinnrl-train --pde burgers --arch fourier --epochs 2000
pinnrl-dashboard

docs.title: When to use a PINN
docs.text:
Be clear about the trade-off. For a well-posed forward problem in one to three dimensions, classical solvers (finite differences, finite elements, spectral methods) are faster and orders of magnitude more accurate. For the 1-D periodic heat equation with \(\alpha = 0.1\) and \(u_0 = \sin(2\pi x)\), an explicit finite-difference scheme on 100 cells reaches a relative L2 error of about \(6 \times 10^{-4}\) in roughly 30 ms of CPU time; a PINN needs minutes of training to reach about \(10^{-2}\).

PINNs earn their place elsewhere:

Situation Why a PINN helps Inverse problems Unknown coefficients or fields are learned jointly with the solution from sparse, noisy measurements. There is no adjoint code to write. Physics plus data Measurements and conservation laws enter the same loss, so gaps in the data are filled by the physics. Awkward geometry or many dimensions It is mesh-free: points are sampled, not meshed. Differentiable surrogates The trained network is a smooth function of (x, t) that is cheap to evaluate and differentiate.

The long-term goal of the project is the first row applied to industry: digital twins that estimate unmeasured states of real process equipment. See Applications and the Research program.

docs.title: Applications: digital twins
docs.text:
A digital twin is a model of a specific physical asset that is kept in sync with that asset through its sensor data. It is used to estimate what can't be measured, to forecast, and to test decisions before applying them. Most industrial twins today are either detailed simulators that are too slow or too rigid to calibrate continuously, or data-driven models that don't respect physics and extrapolate poorly.

PINNs sit between the two. They combine the conservation laws you already know with the sensor streams you already have, and they solve the inverse problem of learning unknown parameters, closures and hidden states as part of training. That is the gap this project targets.

docs.title: Where a PINN fits
docs.text:
The pitch is the same in every row: your plant already logs X. A physics-informed model can turn X into an estimate of Y, which you can't measure continuously, and keep that estimate calibrated as the equipment ages.

Industry Typical twin Physics (PDEs) Where a PINN helps Food and dairy Spray dryers, evaporators, pasteurizers and UHT lines, fermenters Heat and mass transfer, drying kinetics, fouling growth Soft sensors for residual moisture and fouling resistance from routine temperatures and flows; predicting when cleaning-in-place is due Chemicals and petrochemicals Reactors, distillation columns, heat exchangers Reaction–diffusion–convection, heat transfer Identifying kinetic parameters; estimating hot spots and catalyst deactivation from sparse thermocouples Pharma and biopharma Freeze dryers, bioreactors, continuous lines Heat and mass transfer, moving sublimation fronts Product temperature and drying front in freeze-drying from shelf temperature and chamber pressure (process analytical technology) Pulp, paper and textiles Drying sections, coating lines Coupled heat and moisture transport Moisture profiles across the web from a few scanner readings Metals, mining and materials Furnaces, casting, heat treatment, additive manufacturing Heat conduction with phase change (Stefan problems), thermal stress Solidification front and refractory wear from shell temperatures; melt-pool calibration Power and energy Boilers, turbines, nuclear thermal hydraulics, wind farms Heat transfer, fluid flow, structural dynamics Heat-flux and remaining-life estimation; fast wake surrogates for layout and control Batteries and storage EV packs, grid batteries Electrochemistry (single-particle, Doyle–Fuller–Newman models), heat State of health and parameter identification from voltage and temperature curves District heating and HVAC Pipe networks, building energy Transport (advection) in pipes, heat in walls Hidden temperatures and leaks from supply and return sensors Oil, gas and subsurface Reservoirs, pipelines, geothermal Porous-media (Darcy) flow, multiphase pipe flow History matching (permeability inversion); leak localization Aerospace and defense Engines, airframes, thermal protection Fluid flow, structural mechanics, heat Reconstructing full fields from sparse sensors; identifying loads and damage for structural health monitoring Automotive Thermal management, battery packs, aerodynamics Heat, fluid flow Calibrated thermal models; aerodynamic surrogates for design Semiconductors CVD and epitaxy reactors, rapid thermal processing Reaction–diffusion, heat Wafer temperature maps from a few pyrometers; recipe calibration Built environment and infrastructure Buildings, bridges, tunnels, concrete curing Heat and moisture in porous media, structural dynamics Concrete maturity and strength estimation; structural health monitoring Water and environment Treatment plants, rivers, sewers, groundwater Advection–dispersion–reaction, shallow water Identifying contaminant sources; calibrated flood and dispersion models Healthcare Cardiac, vascular and tumor-growth models Reaction–diffusion, blood flow Patient-specific tissue parameters (conductivity, stiffness) from imaging Agriculture Soil, grain storage, greenhouses Richards equation (soil water), heat and moisture Soil hydraulic parameters from probes; hot spots in grain silos

Out of scope: twins without field physics, such as supply-chain, logistics, IT-network and discrete-event production-scheduling twins. Graph, queueing or discrete-event models serve those better than PDEs.

docs.title: What a PINN-based twin is, and isn't
docs.text:
• It is an estimation layer. It sits above the control system (PLC/DCS), reads the historian or OPC UA, and returns estimates with uncertainty and advisory setpoints. It does not replace real-time control loops.
  • It is not a faster CFD. When the physics is fully known and all you need is a forward simulation, use a classical solver.
  • It earns its keep where something important is unmeasured or unknown: a fouling layer, a drying-kinetics curve, a permeability field, a tissue property. Credible deployment also needs a classical baseline (Kalman filters, moving-horizon estimation) for comparison, and calibrated uncertainty.

docs.title: First target: food-powder lines
docs.text:
The first concrete application is the dairy and food-powder line: evaporators feeding spray dryers, as in cheese- and milk-powder plants. The plan:

  1. falling-film evaporator fouling, estimated from effect-level temperatures and flows;
  2. a spray-dryer soft sensor for residual moisture, with a stickiness-margin advisory;
  3. a coupled line-level twin with measurement design (deciding when to pull a lab sample).

This is the research program; its experiments live in experiments/ (track J of the backlog).

docs.title: Benchmarks
docs.text: pinnrl-benchmark has two parts: classical baselines, so PINN accuracy has a reference point, and a multi-seed study that compares collocation samplers fairly. Every number below can be reproduced with the commands shown.

docs.title: Classical baselines
docs.text:
pinnrl-benchmark fdm --pde heat     # explicit finite differences, periodic 1-D heat
pinnrl-benchmark fdm --pde wave     # leap-frog, periodic 1-D travelling wave

Both report the relative L2 error at the final time against the analytical solution, plus the maximum error and the wall time. On the default heat problem (\(\alpha = 0.1\), \(u_0 = \sin 2\pi x\), 101 points), the explicit scheme reaches a relative L2 error of about \(7 \times 10^{-4}\) in about 30 ms. The convergence is second order: doubling the points at a fixed diffusion number cuts the error about four-fold. That's the bar a PINN is measured against on forward problems.

docs.title: Reference solutions
docs.text:
When there is no closed form, PINNs are scored against high-accuracy numerical references (pinnrl.benchmarks.reference):

Reference Method Verification burgers_reference Cole–Hopf integral evaluated by a log-sum-exp trapezoid rule Reproduces Basdevant et al. (1986): \(u_x(0, 1.6037/\pi) = -152.00516\) for \(\nu = 0.01/\pi\); agrees with a fine finite-difference solve to \(7 \times 10^{-5}\) allen_cahn_reference Second-order finite differences plus adaptive Runge–Kutta (method of lines) on a grid 8× finer than the output Grid-converged: doubling the solver grid changes the field by less than \(10^{-5}\) (relative)

docs.title: Sampling study (experiments B01 and B06)
docs.text:
pinnrl-benchmark sampling --seeds 10 --steps 15000 --checkpoints 50 --workers 4

Setup: - The Burgers (\(\nu = 0.01/\pi\)) and Allen–Cahn (\(u_t = 0.001\,u_{xx} + 5(u - u^3)\), \(u_0 = x^2\cos\pi x\)) benchmarks. - A tanh MLP (4 × 64) trained for 15,000 Adam steps on 1,000 points, with 10 paired seeds (identical initial weights across samplers). - Five samplers: - uniform and stratified, with fresh points every step; - uniform refreshed every 100 steps, a control for how often points change; - RAD (k = 1, c = 1) and the RL bandit, also every 100 steps. - Each run records the relative L2 error and the residual evaluations spent, including the sampler's own (RAD +20 %, bandit +0.3 %). Samplers are compared at equal steps (B01) and at equal total evaluations (B06).

PDE Sampler Rel. L2, equal steps vs uniform (paired) Rel. L2, equal evaluations vs uniform Burgers uniform 0.055 – 0.055 – stratified 0.038 6/10, p = 0.63 0.038 6/10, p = 0.63 RAD 0.136 3/10, p = 0.11 0.090 2/10, p = 0.06 RL bandit 0.117 1/10, p = 0.06 0.105 2/10, p = 0.01 (worse) Allen–Cahn uniform 0.568 – 0.568 – RAD 0.533 10/10, p = 0.002 0.547 10/10, p = 0.002 RL bandit 0.520 10/10, p = 0.002 0.518 10/10, p = 0.002

Errors are medians over 10 seeds; "6/10" counts the seeds on which the sampler beat uniform; p is from a Wilcoxon signed-rank test.

What this says:

  • Burgers. No sampler is significantly better than uniform. Seed-to-seed variation (6×) and optimizer noise (the error moves 1.7× between checkpoints at a constant learning rate) swamp any sampling effect. Charged its probe cost, the bandit is significantly worse.
  • Allen–Cahn. Adaptive samplers win on every seed and the bandit gets there with about 40 % fewer evaluations early on. But every method stays stuck near the wrong solution (relative error above 0.5).
  • Recommendation: use uniform (or stratified) by default. Use residual_based (RAD) when the solution has sharp features, and measure it against uniform at equal budget. Treat --rl as experimental.

The full write-up, with IQRs, the same-cadence control and the follow-ups it motivates (optimizer settling, resampling frequency, Allen–Cahn failure modes), is in experiments/B01_sampling_equal_compute.

docs.title: Identification baseline (experiment F01)
docs.text:
python experiments/F01_heat_alpha_recovery/run.py --seeds 10 --steps 5000 --workers 4

The diffusivity of the 1-D heat equation (\(\alpha = 0.1\), started at 0.5) is identified from 20 to 1,000 noisy observations of the exact solution, for noise standard deviations from 0 to 0.1, on 10 seeds. The heat entry of the catalogue is used with alpha trainable; a 4 × 64 MLP trains for 5,000 Adam steps with loss weights residual / BC / IC / data = 1 / 10 / 10 / 10.

Noise σ \(N_{\text{obs}}\) = 20 50 200 1000 0 0.017 0.019 0.020 0.015 0.01 0.027 0.016 0.019 0.017 0.05 0.041 0.033 0.021 0.020 0.1 0.054 0.055 0.024 0.025

Median relative error of \(\hat\alpha\) over 10 seeds.

What this says:

  • A 2 % floor that data cannot lower. With clean or lightly noisy data every seed lands at \(\hat\alpha \approx 0.098\) whatever the number of observations. The Cramér–Rao bound for 1,000 points is 0.2 %, so the floor is the surrogate's own forward error (2–3 % in \(u\)), absorbed by the parameter.
  • Above the floor, near-efficient. For σ ≥ 0.05 the spread of \(\hat\alpha\) across seeds matches the Cramér–Rao bound from the same points to within about 20 %, so the Fisher information predicts how many sensors a target accuracy needs.
  • Few noisy points bias low. At 20 points the bias grows with noise (−3 %, −5 %, −9 %): the physics loss prefers a smoother, slower-diffusing field when the fixed data weight ignores the noise level.
  • Field error does not predict parameter error. The relative L2 error of \(u\) is 2–4 % in every cell while the median error of α spans 1.5–5.5 % and single seeds reach 22 %.

The full write-up, with IQRs, the spread against the bound per cell, and the follow-ups (the floor after optimizer settling, K01 Fisher information, K39 likelihood weighting), is in experiments/F01_heat_alpha_recovery.

Initial guess (experiment F04). Ten starting values from 0.1× to 10× the truth, on one data set per seed (200 observations, noise 0.05). For a fixed data set the ten starts land within 0.3 % of each other, six times less than the spread across seeds; the two seeds that end 5–7 % low do so for every start. Starts far above the truth settle in 700–900 steps, sooner than starts near it. The estimate is a function of the data, not of the guess. Write-up: experiments/F04_initial_guess.

Fixed sensors (experiment F05). Plant-like data: 1, 2, 4 or 8 probes at fixed positions read at regular times, against random scatter, all with 200 observations. One probe at mid-domain has the lowest Cramér–Rao bound (1.2 % at noise 0.05 against 1.7 % for scatter) and the PINN delivers it (median error 1.1 % against 1.9 %), because the information about α sits at mid-domain and late times. Spreading the same readings over 8 positions raises the bound and the measured spread alike. Dense time series also halve the low-noise bias. Write-up: experiments/F05_fixed_sensors.

docs.title: Conditioning diagnostics (experiment K01)
docs.text:
python experiments/K01_fisher_information/run.py --seeds 3

pinnrl.analysis.surrogate_sensitivities computes \(\partial u / \partial\theta\) from a trained network by the implicit-function theorem (matrix-free Hessian blocks, a MINRES solve), and fisher_information turns it into the Cramér–Rao bound. K01 checks this against the exact layer: on heat and the two-parameter KdV soliton the bounds, the α–β correlation and the condition number agree to 1–4 % (Jacobians to 2–6 %). On Burgers at \(\nu = 0.01/\pi\) the network smooths the shock and its bound is 2–25× too optimistic. The surrogate's Fisher information is trusted only where its forward error is small compared with the feature the parameter acts on, and the field error is reported next to it. Write-up: experiments/K01_fisher_information; the live demo is in notebooks/07_conditioning.ipynb.

Two parameters, and a shock (experiments F02, F03). For the KdV soliton with two coefficients the bound says 200 clean points determine (α, β) to 0.6 % and 1.4 %; the PINN returns them 18 % and 25 % low on every seed, and a run started at the truth drifts to the same point: the minimum of the PINN loss is not at the truth, because the network cannot zero the third-derivative residual of the true soliton. A tenfold data weight halves the bias. For the Burgers viscosity at ν = 0.01/π the network resolves a shock several times wider than the real one and reports a viscosity 2.5–5× too large, still falling at 10,000 steps. The surrogate floor therefore orders as heat 2 %, KdV soliton 20 %, Burgers shock 150 %, and above it the spread across seeds still follows the bound. Write-ups: experiments/F02_kdv_joint, experiments/F03_burgers_nu.

Profile likelihood (experiment F07). With α fixed on a grid and the network retrained, the misfit of the exact solution reproduces the Fisher parabola to 2 %, while the PINN's data misfit is 2.5–12× flatter: the network deviates from the PDE instead of reproducing the wrong solution. Profile likelihood with a PINN needs hard physics or the full weighted loss. Write-up: experiments/F07_profile_likelihood.

docs.title: Training conditioning (experiment K03)
docs.text: Across eight operators and two architectures after 3,000 steps, the architecture sets the conditioning, not the operator order: a tanh MLP's residual tangent kernel has a condition number near \(10^8\) for every problem, Fourier features bring it down by three to five orders but make the residual kernel's trace \(10^3\)–\(4 \times 10^3\) times the boundary kernel's on wave-type and fourth-order problems (the gradient pathology), and no run is at a minimum (every Hessian has a negative Ritz value whose size tracks the final loss). Write-up: experiments/K03_training_conditioning; the tools are pinnrl.analysis.loss_hessian_spectrum and tangent_kernel_spectrum.

docs.title: Disturbance and stability (experiments K05–K07)
docs.text: Data disturbances (K05). For the identified heat diffusivity, a sensor bias or a timestamp delay shifts the estimate by the linear prediction \(F^{-1}J^\top\delta y\) to within 20 %, with negligible scatter across seeds; a bias of the noise level moves α by 18 % and nothing in the residual flags it. Dropout of 75 % of the points or of a whole probe costs information, not accuracy. Outliers break the squared-error data term and raise the residual 10–25×, which makes the residual a detector for them. Problem perturbations (K06). A trained field responds to a change of initial data, boundary data or a coefficient as the exact solution does (amplification 0.7–1.2) when the change exceeds the surrogate's own field error, and not at all below it: the field error is the resolution of a trained surrogate. Stability constants (K07). On an independent sample the error falls in proportion to the residual with a constant near 1 for heat, convection, wave, Klein–Gordon and heat in 2-D, and an equation-dependent constant otherwise; for the beam the error stalls while the residual falls, because the boundary and initial mismatches are the binding terms. Write-ups: K05_data_disturbance, K06_problem_disturbance, K07_stability_constants; the tools are pinnrl.analysis.perturb_observations, linear_response and stability_ratio.

docs.title: Calibrated uncertainty (experiments F06, K10, K39, K46)
docs.text: Over 30 synthetic data sets, the interval the Laplace posterior gives for the identified heat diffusivity (the surrogate's Fisher information, pinnrl.uq.laplace_posterior) has a standard deviation equal to the spread of the estimate across data sets to three digits, and covers the truth 77 % of the time instead of 90 % only because every estimate is 2 % low (the surrogate floor). An ensemble over initializations covers 13 %: it measures the initialization noise, a quarter of the data noise. The likelihood-ratio region of the exact misfit sampled by the swarm covers 90 %. Setting the data weight from the Gaussian noise model makes the estimate worse (bias up to −21 % at low weights), because the residual of a trained PINN is a systematic approximation error, not noise; the balance weight is set by the surrogate's floor relative to the noise. On closed-form misfits the swarm's region coincides with the Fisher ellipse at these noise levels and under-samples its edges, which K47 addresses. Write-ups: F06_coverage, K39_likelihood_weighting, K46_swarm_equivalence.

docs.title: Sampling follow-ups (experiments B02, B03, B04, B08)
docs.text: On heat, convection, wave and the KdV soliton no sampler differs significantly from fresh uniform points (errors 0.2–2.5 %, 5 paired seeds); RAD has the best median on three of the four and narrows the spread (B02). On Burgers the resampling cadence changes the error threefold, more than any choice of sampler at a fixed cadence, and RAD's best cadence is every 10 steps, which is now the study's default (B04). Good RAD settings on Burgers lie on \(c \approx k/2\), and a zero uniform floor with a sharp exponent is three times worse than uniform; on Allen–Cahn every setting is equally and modestly better than uniform (B03). The error falls as about \(N^{-1/3}\) in the number of collocation points on Burgers, for uniform and RAD alike, and not at all on Allen–Cahn, while cost is linear in \(N\) (B08). Write-ups: B02_more_pdes, B03_rad_grid, B04_resampling_frequency, B08_point_count.

docs.title: Concepts
docs.text: This page covers the ideas behind each component of pinnrl: what it does and why it is there. Derivations are in the cited papers.

docs.title: The PINN loss
docs.text:
A network \(u_\theta(x, t)\) is trained to satisfy the PDE \(\mathcal{N}[u] = 0\) together with its boundary and initial conditions (Raissi, Perdikaris & Karniadakis, 2019). Derivatives are computed exactly by automatic differentiation, and the loss is a weighted sum:

\[ \mathcal{L}(\theta) = w_r \underbrace{\operatorname{mean}\,\lvert \mathcal{N}[u_\theta] \rvert^2}_{\text{collocation points}} + w_b\,\mathcal{L}_\text{boundary} + w_i\,\mathcal{L}_\text{initial} + w_d\,\mathcal{L}_\text{data} \]

\(\mathcal{L}_\text{boundary}\) averages over every condition on every boundary face, \(\mathcal{L}_\text{initial}\) is taken at \(t = t_0\), and \(\mathcal{L}_\text{data}\) is zero unless observations are attached (inverse and data modes). Each term is a mean squared error with the default loss_function: mse.

Training is ordinary gradient descent on \(\mathcal{L}\). Because nothing ties the network to a mesh, the same code handles irregular domains and higher dimensions. The flip side is that accuracy depends on where the residual is evaluated (sampling), how the terms are balanced (weighting), and what the network can represent (architecture). Those are the three knobs below.

docs.title: Boundary and initial conditions
docs.text:
Kind Enforces Config Dirichlet \(u = g\) on each face dirichlet: {value: 0}, {left: a, right: b}, or {type: exact} (uses the exact solution) Neumann \(\partial u/\partial x_i = g\) on both faces of axis \(i\) (the axis derivative, not the outward normal, so a nonzero \(g\) has the same sign on both faces) neumann: {value: 0} or {type: zero} Periodic \(u\) and \(\partial u/\partial x_i\) match across opposite faces periodic: {}

Every spatial axis gets the condition on both faces. For equations that are second order in time (wave, pendulum), the initial loss also enforces the initial velocity \(u_t(x, t_0)\) (initial_condition.velocity, default 0). Without it the problem is not well posed. Unknown condition types raise an error rather than being silently ignored.

docs.title: Collocation sampling
docs.text:
The residual is only enforced where it is evaluated. Sharp features such as shocks, interfaces and boundary layers occupy a small part of the domain, so uniform points can under-resolve exactly where the error lives.

Strategy Idea Cost uniform A jittered space-time grid, redrawn every batch. Unbiased, and implicitly regularizing. none stratified Latin-hypercube points: one per stratum, so coverage is even. none residual_based (RAD) Draw from a uniform candidate pool (pool_factor = 4 times the batch) with probability \(p(x) \propto \lvert r(x)\rvert^k / \operatorname{mean}\lvert r\rvert^k + c\) (Wu et al., 2023). \(k\) sharpens the focus; \(c\) keeps a uniform floor. The trainer uses \(k = 1\), \(c = 0\); other values are arguments of generate_collocation_points and of the sampling study. one residual evaluation per pool point adaptive (RL bandit, experimental) A DQN with discount 0, i.e. a contextual bandit, learns which of 16 × 8 space-time cells have high residual from probes, and mixes its picks 50/50 with uniform points. 1-D only. 256 residual evaluations (32 cells × 8 points) per update, every probe_every batches (10 in config.yaml)

Adaptive sampling is not free: it has to pay for its overhead and beat a strong uniform baseline at equal budget. Benchmarks reports how the strategies compare.

docs.title: Architectures
docs.text:
Plain MLPs suffer from spectral bias: they learn low-frequency components first and struggle with high-frequency or multiscale solutions (Rahaman et al., 2019). Most of the alternatives exist to counter it.

Key Idea Use it for feedforward Tanh MLP, the standard PINN baseline smooth solutions; the first thing to try resnet MLP blocks with skip connections deeper networks that still train stably fourier Random Fourier features \([\sin(Bz), \cos(Bz)]\) of \(z = (x, t)\) before the MLP, with a fixed \(B_{ij} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)\) and \(\sigma\) = scale, which sets the frequency band (Tancik et al., 2020); one hidden layer per hidden_dims entry oscillatory or high-frequency solutions siren Layers \(\sin\big(\omega_0 (W z + b)\big)\) with frequency omega_0 (Sitzmann et al., 2020) wave-like solutions; sensitive to omega_0 fno Fourier-neural-operator-style spectral layers applied to point-wise inputs (Li et al., 2021): the FFT runs over each point's hidden features. This is not operator learning: it maps \((x, t)\) to \(u\), not functions to functions. experimentation attention Self-attention blocks over a learned embedding experimentation autoencoder An encoder–latent–decoder MLP experimentation

docs.title: Optimizers
docs.text:
• Adam is the robust default.
  • L-BFGS is quasi-Newton with a strong-Wolfe line search. Each step works on one sampled batch, so it behaves best with a single batch per epoch (batch_size = num_collocation_points). It often sharpens the final convergence of smooth problems but can stall early.
  • adam_lbfgs runs Adam for a fraction of the epochs (adam_lbfgs_switch_ratio) and then switches to L-BFGS, a common recipe in the PINN literature.
  • Learning-rate schedules: cosine, reduce_lr (on plateau) or constant, with optional linear warmup.

docs.title: Loss weighting
docs.text:
The residual, boundary and initial terms can differ by orders of magnitude in value and in gradient size. When they do, gradient descent effectively ignores the small ones. Fixed weights (loss_weights) are the simplest fix. The adaptive strategies rebalance during training:

  • lrw: gradient-norm balancing. With \(\bar g_i\) a running average (factor alpha) of \(\lVert \nabla_\theta \mathcal{L}_i \rVert\), the weights are \(w_i \propto 1/(\bar g_i + \epsilon)\), normalized to sum to 1, so no term dominates the update. This is a simplified form of the learning-rate annealing of Wang, Teng & Perdikaris (2021), which scales each term by the ratio of the residual's maximum gradient to that term's mean gradient.
  • rbw: relative loss balancing. The weights are proportional to a running average of each term's loss, normalized to sum to 1 and smoothed again over steps, so the terms with the largest loss get the most weight.

Both replace the loss_weights of the residual, boundary and initial terms; the data weight stays fixed. They are switched off during L-BFGS, where the three terms then have weight 1.

The loss_function setting can be mse (default), mae or huber. The robust losses reduce the influence of outliers, for example noisy observations.

docs.title: Inverse problems
docs.text: Mark PDE parameters as trainable and supply observations. The parameters become torch.nn.Parameters, and a data term \(\mathcal{L}_\text{data} = \operatorname{mean} \lvert u_\theta(x_\text{obs}, t_\text{obs}) - u_\text{obs} \rvert^2\) is added. The parameters enter through the residual (and, for some initial conditions such as the Allen–Cahn and KdV profiles, through the initial loss), so the physics terms pin them to values under which the network solves the PDE, while the data term pulls the solution toward the measurements. Both are optimized together. See Inverse problems.

docs.title: Training modes
docs.text: mode Loss terms Use forward residual + BC + IC Solve a known PDE inverse residual + BC + IC + data, with trainable parameters Identify parameters from data data_augmented residual + BC + IC + data Fit reference data while respecting the physics data_only data A neural surrogate of a dataset (e.g. The Well)
